description: Covers the core techniques for rewiring linked list pointers in-place: full and partial reversal, using a dummy head node to simplify edge cases, and merging/reordering multiple lists — all without converting to an array (O(1) extra space).
important_details: Always draw the pointer rewiring on paper first (prev/curr/next) — off-by-one pointer bugs are the most common failure mode.
A dummy node placed before the real head eliminates special-casing 'the head itself changes' (removal, insertion, merging).
Reversal is the building block for many other patterns: palindrome checks, reordering, and add-two-numbers style problems.
Two-pass (count length first) vs one-pass (fast/slow) solutions both appear frequently — know when each is asked for.
other_relevant_details: This pattern pairs heavily with Fast & Slow Pointers (finding the middle/nth-from-end) — many hard linked-list problems combine both techniques in one solution.

variations.description: Iteratively re-point each node's 'next' to its predecessor using three tracking pointers (prev, curr, next), producing a fully reversed list in one O(n) pass.
important_details: Save curr.next BEFORE overwriting curr.next = prev, or the rest of the list is lost.
prev starts as null (it becomes the new tail's next); the loop ends when curr is null and prev is the new head.
A recursive version exists too but uses O(n) call-stack space — mention the trade-off in interviews.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) iterative (O(n) if recursive).

variations.variation: Reverse a Sublist / Reverse in Groups of K
variations.description: Reverse only a bounded segment of the list (positions m to n, or every consecutive group of k nodes), requiring careful reconnection of the reversed segment back to the untouched parts of the list.
important_details: Use a dummy node before the segment so you always have a stable 'node before the reversal' to reconnect to, even if the segment starts at the head.
For group-of-k reversal, first check that at least k nodes remain — if fewer remain, leave that final partial group unreversed (per the classic problem statement).
Track four pointers conceptually: the node before the segment, the segment's original head (which becomes the new tail), the segment's new head, and the node after the segment.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n). Space: O(1) iterative version (the recursive sample above uses O(n/k) stack frames).

variations.description: Prepend a placeholder 'dummy' node before the real head so that insertion, deletion, or merge logic never needs a special case for 'the head node itself is changing'.
important_details: Always return dummy.next at the end, never the original head variable (which may have been removed or is no longer first).
Especially useful for 'remove Nth from end', 'remove all nodes with value X', and merge/partition problems.
Combine with fast/slow pointers for the 'Nth from end' family: advance fast n steps ahead of slow, starting both from dummy.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(n), single pass. Space: O(1).

problems.name: Remove Nth Node From End of List
Remove Duplicates from Sorted List II

variations.description: Combine or interleave two or more linked lists into a single list, either by merging two sorted lists node-by-node or by reordering a single list's nodes (e.g., alternating front/back).
important_details: Merging two sorted lists is the merge-step of merge sort applied directly to linked lists — O(1) space unlike arrays.
For k-way merge, a min-heap of the current head of each list gives O(N log k) instead of O(N*k) pairwise merging.
Reordering (e.g., L0→Ln→L1→Ln-1...) typically combines find-middle + reverse-second-half + merge-alternately.
variations.other_relevant_details: Time Complexity: O(m + n) for two lists; O(N log k) for k-way merge with a heap. Space: O(1) for two-list merge, O(k) for the heap.
